passage:
Dear Manjula,
You asked what to say when you visit Farida's family next week. I learnt something this month, so let me tell you.
When Mr D'Souza downstairs died, I panicked about words. I rehearsed three sentences on the stairs and forgot all of them at the door. So I just held out the dal and rice. Mrs D'Souza took the dish and said, "Nobody has eaten since yesterday."
After that the colony found its jobs without any meeting. Rafiq uncle handled the chairs. The Nair girls took the grandchildren to the park. I came every evening at seven to wash the steel glasses and sit in a corner. Some evenings nobody spoke to me at all.
Last Sunday she held my wrist and said, "You came every day." Not one word about anything I'd said.
So go, Manju. Take something. Stay a while.
Your akka,
Chandrika

qa.q: What did Chandrika bring to the D'Souza home?
qa.a: Chandrika held out the dal and rice.

qa.q: How did Chandrika feel at the door the first time?
qa.a: She was nervous and panicky about saying the right thing, and forgot all three sentences she had rehearsed.

qa.q: What does Chandrika advise Manjula, and why is it wise?
qa.a: To go, take something and stay a while, because being present and doing small tasks mattered more to Mrs D'Souza than perfect words.

qa.q: How did Mrs D'Souza experience Chandrika's evening visits?
qa.a: She felt cared for by the steady presence; what she remembered was "You came every day", not anything that was said.

grounding: Chandrika's letter shows an adult supporting a bereaved family with food, presence and small tasks rather than perfect words.

passage:
Monday: new flat, new room. Francis, two, cried at bedtime and kicked his blanket off three times. Papa Anand tried a new storybook; Francis pushed it away.
Wednesday: Anand went back to the old way: bath, the same blue cup of milk, Mama switching off the big light, and the moon song, twice. Francis hummed along through a yawn.
Saturday: at the first line of the moon song, Francis climbed into bed by himself and patted the pillow for Papa.

qa.q: What song did Anand sing at bedtime?
qa.a: Anand sang the moon song, twice.

qa.q: Why did Francis push the new storybook away on Monday?
qa.a: He was probably unsettled and upset in the new room, and a new story felt strange rather than comforting.

qa.q: What helped Francis settle, and why?
qa.a: Going back to the same bath, blue cup, light and moon song made bedtime predictable, so Francis felt safe.

qa.q: What might bedtime be like for Anand once the routine works?
qa.a: He is likely relieved and feels close to Francis, since bedtime is now calm instead of a struggle.

grounding: Shows a toddler settling more easily once the same bedtime sequence returns each night, making the new home feel safe.

passage: The power went out just as the family gathered to set up the Christmas crib. Grandma lit candles. Five-year-old Maria held the tiny baby figure very carefully in both hands. "Not yet," whispered her cousin Jahnavi. "Baby comes at midnight." Maria nodded seriously and waited, clutching it. When everyone sang a carol in the dark, she sang the words she knew, loudly, and hummed the rest. At midnight Grandma said, "Now, Maria." She laid the baby in the straw, then looked round at everyone. "I did it right!" Uncle clapped, and Maria clapped too.

qa.q: Who lit the candles when the power went out?
qa.a: Grandma lit candles.

qa.q: How can you tell Maria wanted to do the custom properly?
qa.a: She waited seriously, clutching the figure until midnight, and announced "I did it right!", which shows she felt proud and grown-up.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi help Maria join in?
qa.a: Jahnavi whispered the family rule, that the baby comes at midnight, so Maria knew what to do.

qa.q: What might Grandma feel when Maria lays the baby in the straw?
qa.a: She is likely happy and touched to see the youngest carrying on the family's Christmas custom.

grounding: Shows a young child joining a family Christmas custom and delighting in doing it right, which makes her feel one of the family.

passage: On the terrace of Block C in their Chennai colony, Vijay, Chandrika and Imran invented the Tank Club, named after the water tank they sat under. The rules: meet at five, the password is "rasam", and the handshake is two slaps, a thumb twist and a pretend sneeze. Vijay practised the sneeze in the mirror at home. On Thursday a new boy, Joel, climbed the stairs and asked to join. The three looked at one another. Chandrika said, "You have to know the password." Joel didn't. He stood there awkwardly, then went back down. Vijay felt big for a moment, then strangely bad. The next day he taught Joel the handshake behind the stairwell, sneeze and all.

qa.q: What was the Tank Club's password?
qa.a: The password is "rasam".

qa.q: What did Vijay feel after Joel went back downstairs?
qa.a: He felt important for a moment, then strangely bad, as if the club's rule had been unkind.

qa.q: How could the Tank Club keep its fun without shutting others out?
qa.a: They could keep the handshake and password but teach them to newcomers like Joel, as Vijay did, so the ritual welcomes instead of excludes.

qa.q: What was it like for Joel on the terrace without the password?
qa.a: Joel probably felt awkward and left out, facing a club where a made-up word decided who belonged.

grounding: Shows children inventing a club with a password and handshake that marks who belongs and who does not.

passage: The train to Ajmer was four hours late, and the Jaipur platform was an oven. Yusuf's family sat on their bags: Ammi, Abbu, two little sisters, Dadi fanning herself with a folded newspaper. Every year they went to tie a thread at the dargah for Dadi's wish. Yusuf, sixteen, scrolled back through his chat with Usha from class. "Do you actually believe the thread does anything?" she had asked. He hadn't answered. He didn't know. Watching Dadi mouth a prayer with her eyes closed, he felt two things at once: love, and a small stubborn doubt. When the train finally came, he carried Dadi's bag to their seats and asked, gently, "Dadi, what do you ask for when you tie it?" She laughed. "That you all come with me next year too."

qa.q: How late was the train to Ajmer?
qa.a: The train was four hours late.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling as he watched Dadi pray?
qa.a: He felt torn, holding love for Dadi alongside a small stubborn doubt about the thread.

qa.q: Why was Yusuf's question to Dadi a good way to explore his doubt?
qa.a: He asked gently and with curiosity rather than to argue, so Dadi could share what the ritual means to her.

qa.q: What might the ritual mean to Dadi, going by her answer?
qa.a: For her it seems to be as much about keeping the family together as about the thread, since her wish is that they all come again.

grounding: Shows a teenager feeling both love for his family and doubt about an inherited ritual, and asking a respectful question.

passage:
"Fresher! Up on the chair. Sing the song, and after every line say 'I am nothing'." Akash grinned. Six seniors crowded the corridor, phones out.
"Why?" Tenzin asked.
"Because that's how you become one of us. We all did it."
"Everyone does it, bro," muttered Karan, the other fresher, already climbing onto a chair.
Tenzin's face burned. He wanted the Saturday football, the jokes at mess, a nickname of his own. "I'll play on your team. I'll carry the kit. I'm not doing this."
"Then enjoy eating alone for four years."
That night Tenzin knocked on the warden's door. "Sir, they're making freshers do things on video. Karan too."
Mr Lobo put down his pen. "Thank you for telling me. You've done nothing wrong. I'm coming to the corridor now, and those videos will be deleted tonight."

qa.q: How many seniors crowded the corridor?
qa.a: Six seniors crowded the corridor, phones out.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when Akash ordered him onto the chair?
qa.a: He wanted badly to belong, the football, the jokes, a nickname, but felt humiliated by the task, so the wish and the refusal pulled against each other.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do that protected himself and others?
qa.a: He offered fair ways to belong, refused the humiliating task, and told the warden that same night, mentioning that Karan was involved too.

qa.q: How might Karan be feeling as he climbs onto the chair?
qa.a: Karan may feel scared and resigned, going along because refusing seems to cost more than the humiliation.

grounding: Shows a new student pressed to do humiliating tasks to belong, refusing, and a warden acting the same night.

subtype: Missing home rituals abroad or in a hostel [Receiver]
passage: Diwali morning in Leeds came with grey drizzle and a nine o'clock exam. Saurabh woke at six out of habit. At home, Maa would be drawing the rangoli by now, Papa arguing with the fairy lights, his sister sneaking sweets from the box before prayers. Here there was only the hum of the hostel fridge. He stood in the shared kitchen, homesick in a way that surprised him, and lit a single tea-light on the windowsill. Farida from across the corridor came in for coffee and saw it. "Is it today?" He nodded. She vanished, then came back with her flatmate Ece and a box of dates. "Five minutes before your exam," Farida said. "We'll make it a thing." They stood round the tiny flame, three people and a humming fridge. Ece asked if she could light the next one.

qa.q: What time was Saurabh's exam?
qa.a: His exam was at nine o'clock.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling in the shared kitchen?
qa.a: He felt homesick in a way that surprised him, missing the rangoli, the lights and the sweets at home.

qa.q: Why did the tea-light help Saurabh feel more anchored?
qa.a: It was a small new ritual that kept a piece of home, and sharing it with Farida and Ece turned it into something he belonged to here.

qa.q: How might Farida see the tiny flame on the windowsill?
qa.a: She likely read it as a sign he was missing home, and wanted to make his morning less lonely by joining in.

grounding: Shows a young man abroad missing festival mornings at home and creating a small new ritual with hostel friends.

subtype: Creating new rituals in a new life [Actor]
passage:
"Four people eating lunch at four different desks," Tejas said, looking round the tiny office. "Is it always like this?"
Elizabeth didn't look up from her screen. "Since before I joined. Everyone's busy."
"What if, Fridays at four, we stop for chai? Fifteen minutes. I'll make it."
Mohan from accounts snorted. "Chai committee. Very serious."
"Very serious," Tejas agreed. "Attendance compulsory, complaints allowed."
The first Friday, only Elizabeth came, mostly to be polite. The second Friday, Mohan wandered in "just for the biscuits".
The fourth Friday, Elizabeth brought her grandmother's lemon cake. "We're doing this properly now," she said.
Mohan raised his cup. "To the chai committee."
"Same time next week?" Tejas asked.
"Obviously," said Elizabeth. "Where else will I complain about my week?"

qa.q: When did Tejas suggest stopping for chai?
qa.a: Fridays at four, for fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What might Tejas have been hoping for when he suggested the chai break?
qa.a: He probably felt a little lonely in a silent office and hoped a shared break would make them feel like a team.

qa.q: What helped the chai break catch on?
qa.a: Tejas kept it light and regular, made the chai himself, and let people come for their own reasons until it became theirs too.

qa.q: How has Elizabeth's view of the chai break changed?
qa.a: She came first only to be polite, but by the fourth Friday she brings cake and treats it as the place to share her week.

grounding: Shows a newly employed adult starting a weekly team chai that turns separate colleagues into a small community.

subtype: Attending a ritual without full belief [Observer]
passage:
Before. On Tuesday, Mohit told his sister Avni on the phone, "I'll come for Dadaji's barsi puja, but I'm not pretending I believe the priest's part." "Nobody asked you to pretend," she said. "Just come."
During. On Saturday, in the crowded front room, Mohit sat near the edge. He watched Dadi's lips move with the Sanskrit, word for word, her hand steady on the brass lamp. Chachaji, who never cried, wiped his eyes during the offering. When the priest asked the grandsons to pour water, Mohit did it slowly and carefully, without mouthing any mantra.
After. On Monday Dadi phoned him. "You poured it well, beta." "Dadi, I don't really believe all of it." "I know," she said. "You came. That's what I'll remember."

qa.q: What did the priest ask the grandsons to do?
qa.a: The priest asked the grandsons to pour water.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling as he watched Dadi and Chachaji during the puja?
qa.a: He was moved and quietly respectful, seeing how much the ritual meant to them even though he didn't share the belief.

qa.q: How did Mohit take part without pretending or showing contempt?
qa.a: He poured the water slowly and carefully but didn't mouth mantras, and later told Dadi honestly that he didn't believe all of it.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Mohit's presence at the puja?
qa.a: For her, his coming mattered more than his belief; she already knew, and what she will remember is that he came.

grounding: Mohit attends a family ritual he does not fully share, sees what it means to the elders, and takes part with respect and honesty.
